periods.activity_title: Into the Tunnel: Reading and Discussing Suraj's World

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.144): discuss Suraj's comparison of the train to a magical creature and the watchman's tunnel routine.

homework.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.149): answer the five questions on Part II of the story — the leopard and the night mail.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the story aloud from p.140 to p.144 with students following in their textbooks, pausing briefly at key moments — the train's approach, Suraj's walk through the tunnel, the flash of orange on the hillside. Students listen and note any words or images that stand out to them.

Class discussion on “Let us discuss” (p.144): students identify the phrases Suraj uses to compare the train to a magical creature, then trace the clues that told him the train was close. Teacher invites two or three students to share their chosen phrases before the class agrees on the most evocative ones.

Students examine the flow-chart question on p.144 about the watchman's inspection system in pairs, reconstructing the sequence of steps Sunder Singh follows by day and by night. Teacher draws the chart on the board and pairs share their answers to complete it together.

periods.teacher_notes: The prose is richly sensory — draw attention to Bond's sound imagery (the whistle, the roar, the creak) as students follow the shared reading, since this language feeds directly into the vocabulary work on sound words later in the chapter. A common pitfall is treating Sunder Singh's remark about ‘lending’ the tunnel to the Government as humorous throwaway dialogue; prompt students to consider what it reveals about his sense of ownership and belonging. Students who find the flow-chart unfamiliar may need a quick model of one step before working in pairs.

periods.activity_title: Reflecting on Courage and Listening for Directions

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.150–151): discuss what draws Sunder Singh and Suraj together and why Sunder Singh is called a ‘firefly’.
Let us listen (p.176): listen to the museum audio guide and mark the treasure-hunt route on the map.

time_bands.activity: Teacher continues the shared reading from p.144 to p.148 (Part II of the story) at a measured pace, then leads a focused discussion on the ‘Let us think and reflect’ questions (p.150–151): what draws the old watchman and the young boy together, and what the image of Sunder Singh as a ‘firefly’ suggests about his role in the dark jungle. Students offer short spoken responses before the teacher draws out the themes of courage and unlikely friendship.

Teacher explains the museum treasure-hunt context from ‘Let us listen’ (p.176) and distributes or draws the museum map outline on the board. The audio guide transcript is read aloud twice at a natural pace while students listen and trace the route, marking the rooms they pass through to locate the treasure.
Quick whole-class check: teacher asks one student to narrate the route aloud and another to name the room where the treasure is hidden, confirming the correct path together.

periods.teacher_notes: Bond's closing image — Suraj glimpsing Sunder Singh's lamp from the night mail — is the emotional hinge of the story; give students a moment to visualise that scene before the discussion begins, as it anchors the ‘firefly’ question concretely. For the listening task, read the audio guide at a steady pace and allow students to pause their pencil between rooms — rushing the transcript is the most common reason students lose the route at the Weapons Room turn. Students who finish marking early can label the rooms they passed through.
materials: Museum map (drawn on board or photocopied)

periods.activity_title: Giving Directions and Writing a Train Journey

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (p.144 area): role-play Anju and the tour manager giving and following directions to the trekking site.
Let us write (p.148): write a descriptive paragraph about a personal train journey — sights, sounds, and feelings.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly reviews the direction phrases from the ‘Let us speak’ box (turn left, keep going straight till, take the roundabout, etc.) by reading them aloud and asking the class to echo each phrase, so every student has the vocabulary ready before pair work begins.

Students work in pairs for the ‘Let us speak’ role-play: Student A plays Anju on a call to the tour manager, marking the map as Student B gives directions from the railway station to the trekking site. After an unhurried exchange, pairs swap roles so both students practise giving and following directions. Teacher circulates and prompts hesitant speakers with a direction phrase from the box.

Teacher models the writing task from ‘Let us write’ (p.148) by narrating two or three sentences aloud — how boarding the train felt, one sound, one sight — then students write their own descriptive paragraph guided by the four prompts (boarding, sounds, sights, feelings). Students draft, reread silently, and make one revision before the teacher invites a volunteer to share.
One or two students read their opening sentences aloud; teacher offers brief oral feedback on the most vivid detail in each, ending the writing activity with positive reinforcement.

periods.teacher_notes: In the speaking role-play, students often drop the direction phrases and just point at the map — insist that Student B speaks every instruction aloud, as the map is for Student A to mark, not for Student B to indicate. For the writing task, Bond's own prose offers a ready model: the sounds Suraj hears (the hiss of steam, the creak of the jungle) can inspire students who feel they have ‘nothing to describe’. Encourage students to write from a specific moment rather than summarising the whole journey.
materials: Textbook (map and direction-phrase box for speaking task)
Lined paper or notebooks for writing

periods.activity_title: Sound Words, Past Habits, and the World Beyond the Tunnel

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.151–152): match the five sound words to their meanings, then complete the sentences using their correct forms.
Let us learn (p.152–153): understand ‘would’ for past habits and complete the fill-in exercise using ‘used to’ or ‘would’.
Let us explore (p.153): discuss the Atal Tunnel and the history of Indian Railways; students share one fact they find remarkable.

homework.task_brief: Let us learn (p.153): punctuate the Charminar paragraph using brackets, semicolons, and colons.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes ‘creaking’, ‘chatter’, ‘hissing’, ‘rustle’, and ‘puffing’ on the board and asks students to predict their meanings from the story's context before consulting the matching task on p.151. After individual matching, the class confirms answers together, then students complete the sentence fill-in exercise on p.152 using the correct forms of the same words.

Teacher reads the grammar explanation on p.152 aloud — how ‘would’ signals a habitual past action in the watchman's routine — and asks students to identify one more ‘would’ example from the story. Students then complete the fill-in exercise on p.153 using ‘used to’ or ‘would’, with teacher guidance on the key distinction (an action that no longer happens calls for ‘used to’ when a state is implied).

Teacher briefly introduces the ‘Let us explore’ content (p.153): the Atal Tunnel's record length and the 1853 first Indian passenger train journey. Students share one fact or question each in a quick round — connecting the tunnel in the story to real-world engineering and railway history — before the teacher closes with a brief reflection on what Ruskin Bond's story says about human connection to these structures.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently confuse ‘used to’ and ‘would’ when a state verb (be, live) is involved — ‘would be’ for states sounds unnatural in English, so model the contrast explicitly with an example from the story before the fill-in begins. For the sound-words matching, encourage students to say each word aloud so the phonetic quality of ‘hissing’ and ‘creaking’ guides them toward the correct meaning. The ‘Let us explore’ discussion is deliberately open-ended; accept any factual response about railways or tunnels and redirect fanciful claims gently.

items.source_lo: Student analyses character, theme, and authorial intent using prose narrative as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Suraj's curiosity inside the tunnel, Sunder Singh's sense of ownership, courage in the dark, their unlikely friendship, the firefly image.
items.item_stem: In the story, Sunder Singh tells Suraj that he has ‘lent’ the tunnel to the Government. Which of the following best explains what this remark reveals about Sunder Singh?

options.label: A
options.text: He feels a deep sense of ownership and belonging to the tunnel and the jungle around it.

options.label: B
options.text: He is telling Suraj that he will ask for the tunnel back when he retires.

options.label: C
options.text: He is unhappy that the Government took over the tunnel without paying him.

options.label: D
options.text: He wants Suraj to understand that the tunnel is a Government building and must be respected.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Students who choose this read the remark as a complaint about compensation rather than as an expression of deep personal attachment.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Suggests a literal reading — the student misses the proprietary affection and playful irony in Sunder Singh's phrasing.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Introduces a future intention not present in the story; the student is extending the remark beyond what the text supports.

items.source_lo: Student analyses character, theme, and authorial intent using prose narrative as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Suraj's curiosity inside the tunnel, Sunder Singh's sense of ownership, courage in the dark, their unlikely friendship, the firefly image.
items.item_stem: At the close of the story, Suraj spots the distant glow of Sunder Singh's lamp from the night mail and feels a quiet warmth toward his friend. Bond describes the watchman as a kind of ‘firefly’ in the dark jungle. What does this image suggest about Sunder Singh's role in the story, and how does it connect to the theme of courage that runs through the narrative? Write your answer in three to four sentences.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The firefly image suggests that Sunder Singh is a small but vital source of light in an otherwise dark and lonely place, guiding trains safely through the tunnel and giving warmth to the jungle around him. Just as a firefly shines without fanfare, Sunder Singh performs his brave, quiet duty — walking the dark tunnel, confronting the leopard — without seeking recognition. This connects to the story's theme that courage need not be dramatic; it can be the steady, daily act of one person lighting the dark for others.

items.source_lo: Student follows spoken directional instructions and maps a route using listening as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Museum treasure-hunt audio guide: entrance hall, art gallery, decorative art, weapons room, musical instruments, auditorium.
items.item_stem: Listen to the museum audio guide. Which of the following correctly describes the route from the Art Gallery to the room where the treasure is hidden?

options.label: A
options.text: First door on the left from the Art Gallery → Decorative Art Gallery → Musical Instruments Section → second room on the left → Auditorium.

options.label: B
options.text: Second door from the Art Gallery → Musical Instruments Section → turn right → Auditorium.

options.label: C
options.text: Third door on the right from the Art Gallery → Weapons Room → turn left → Musical Instruments Section → second room on the left → Auditorium.

options.label: D
options.text: Third door on the right from the Art Gallery → Weapons Room → turn right → Auditorium.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student correctly identified the Decorative Art Gallery door (first on the left) but applied it as the route to the treasure, confusing two separate doors from the Art Gallery.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student missed the Weapons Room step and invented a direct path; suggests they lost the sequence after the Art Gallery.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student identified the correct door and room (Weapons Room) but turned right instead of left, indicating a direction error at the final navigation step.

items.source_lo: Student follows spoken directional instructions and maps a route using listening as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Museum treasure-hunt audio guide: entrance hall, art gallery, decorative art, weapons room, musical instruments, auditorium.
items.item_stem: Based on the museum audio guide, the second door leading out of the Art Gallery is described as temporarily closed. A visitor who arrived at the Art Gallery and found all three doors unlocked would not know which door to avoid. In two to three sentences, explain why including this kind of information in a spoken guide matters, and describe what a listener should do when a spoken instruction refers to a landmark that may not be visible.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Including details about closed or unavailable routes in a spoken guide is important because a listener cannot see ahead and must rely entirely on what they hear to navigate safely. When a spoken instruction refers to a landmark that may not be visible — such as a closed door — the listener should use the other landmarks mentioned (such as the door's position: left, right, or middle) to identify it by process of elimination rather than by sight.

items.item_stem: You are the tour manager. Anju has just arrived at the railway station and calls you for directions to the trekking site. Using the map in your textbook and at least four direction phrases, give Anju clear spoken directions from the railway station to the trekking site. Your partner will listen and mark the route.

expected_elements: Uses at least four direction phrases correctly (e.g., turn left, keep going straight).
Gives instructions in a logical, step-by-step sequence.
Names landmarks or reference points to help the listener track the route.
Speaks clearly at a pace the listener can follow and mark on the map.

items.source_lo: Student gives and follows spoken directional instructions using role-play as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Anju and the tour manager: directions from a railway station to a trekking site using a map and direction phrases.
items.item_stem: After reaching the trekking site, Anju realises she has taken a wrong turn. She calls the tour manager again and says she is now standing near the roundabout but is unsure which way to go. As the tour manager, respond to her with revised directions, explaining why the earlier route went wrong and giving her corrected instructions. Your partner plays Anju and must ask at least one follow-up question to confirm the route.

expected_elements: Identifies a likely point of confusion and corrects it with a reason.
Gives revised directions from the roundabout using precise direction language.
Responds to the partner's follow-up question clearly and helpfully.
Maintains a natural conversational tone appropriate to a phone call.

items.source_lo: Student writes a descriptive paragraph drawing on personal experience using guided writing as the vehicle.
items.source_context: A personal train journey — boarding, sounds of wheels and whistle, changing scenery, feelings of excitement or curiosity.
items.item_stem: Write a descriptive paragraph about boarding a train. Begin with the moment you arrive at the platform and describe what you hear, see, and feel as the train pulls in and you find your seat. Use at least three specific details — one sound, one sight, and one feeling — to make the scene vivid. Your paragraph should be six to eight sentences.

expected_elements: Opens with a specific moment on the platform or as the train arrives.
Includes at least one vivid sound detail (whistle, wheels, announcements).
Includes at least one specific sight and one feeling.
Sentences are varied in length and the writing flows naturally.

items.source_lo: Student writes a descriptive paragraph drawing on personal experience using guided writing as the vehicle.
items.source_context: A personal train journey — boarding, sounds of wheels and whistle, changing scenery, feelings of excitement or curiosity.
items.item_stem: Imagine you are on a long overnight train journey, like Suraj travelling to Delhi with his father in the story. Write a paragraph describing what you observe and feel as the train moves through the dark countryside at night. You may describe the changing scenery outside, the sounds inside the carriage, and any moment of wonder or quiet reflection you experience. Your paragraph should reveal something about your mood or your thoughts — not just what you see.

expected_elements: Setting is clearly night and conveys a mood of quietness or wonder.
At least one specific sensory detail (sound, sight, or feeling) is included.
Writing reveals the narrator's inner state, not only external observations.
Tone is reflective or imaginative, not merely a factual list of events.

items.item_stem: Match each sound word from the story with its correct meaning.
items.visual_stimulus:
Word | Meaning
creaking | making a long low sound when a wooden object moves
hissing | making a continuous noise like a long 's' sound
rustle | a soft, dry sound made by movement of leaves or paper
chatter | repeated short high sounds made by birds or monkeys
puffing | blowing with short, quick blasts as the wind does

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: creaking – making a long low sound when a wooden object moves; hissing – making a continuous noise like a long 's' sound; rustle – a soft, dry sound made by movement of leaves or paper; chatter – repeated short high sounds made by birds or monkeys; puffing – blowing with short, quick blasts as the wind does.

answer_key.right: making a long low sound when a wooden object moves
making a continuous noise like a long 's' sound
a soft, dry sound made by movement of leaves or paper
repeated short high sounds made by birds or monkeys
blowing with short, quick blasts as the wind does

items.item_stem:
The sentences below describe Sunder Singh's daily routine and the jungle around the tunnel. Choose either 'used to' or 'would' to complete each sentence correctly. Write your choice in the blank provided.

1. Before every train, Sunder Singh __________ (walk) the full length of the tunnel to check for danger.
2. When Suraj was younger, his family __________ (live) near a forest, so he knew the sounds of the jungle well.
3. Every evening, the watchman __________ (light) his lamp and begin his inspection.
4. Leopards __________ (visit) the tunnel area regularly, and Sunder Singh had grown used to their presence.
5. As a child, Suraj __________ (be) afraid of the dark, but his curiosity was stronger than his fear.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. would walk  2. used to live  3. would light  4. would visit  5. used to be

items.source_lo: Student connects a prose text to real-world interdisciplinary knowledge using inquiry as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Atal Tunnel (world's longest highway tunnel above 10,000 feet); Indian Railways history since 1853 first passenger train.
items.item_stem:
Read the two facts below and answer the question that follows.

Fact 1: The Atal Tunnel is 9.02 kilometres long and runs under the Rohtang Pass. It holds the record for being the world's longest highway tunnel above 10,000 feet.
Fact 2: India's first passenger train ran between Bori Bunder (Mumbai) and Thane on 16 April 1853 — over 165 years ago.

Which of the following statements about Indian engineering and transport history is best supported by both facts?

options.label: A
options.text: India built its railway network entirely before building any road tunnels.

options.label: B
options.text: India has a long and continuing tradition of building ambitious transport infrastructure.

options.label: C
options.text: India's transport achievements are mainly confined to the western region of the country.

options.label: D
options.text: The Rohtang Pass was chosen for the tunnel because it was the site of India's first railway station.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Students who choose this impose a chronological sequence not stated in either fact; they are confusing the order of mentioning with the order of construction.
what_each_option_reveals.D: This conflates two separate facts — Rohtang Pass (tunnel location) and Bori Bunder (railway history) — introducing a connection neither fact supports.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Overgeneralises from Bori Bunder being in Mumbai; the facts do not restrict India's achievements to any one region.

items.source_lo: Student connects a prose text to real-world interdisciplinary knowledge using inquiry as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Atal Tunnel (world's longest highway tunnel above 10,000 feet); Indian Railways history since 1853 first passenger train.
items.item_stem: In the story, the railway tunnel through the forested hill is a small but vital link between two parts of the landscape — and between Suraj and Sunder Singh. The Atal Tunnel and the 1853 Bori Bunder–Thane railway line are real examples of how transport structures have connected people and places in India. Design a short research task (five to seven sentences) in which you identify one transport structure in your state or region, describe what it connects, and explain how it has changed life for people who use it. Suggest one source where you would look for information about it.

expected_elements: Names a real transport structure in a known region or state.
Describes clearly what two places or communities the structure connects.
Explains at least one way it has changed daily life for users.
Suggests a plausible and accessible source for further research.
